newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-AGL details access to its gas network.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-AGL details access to its gas network.

text.p: The Australian Gas Light Co (AGL) released on Wednesday details of its undertaking to allow natural gas owned by third parties to be distributed through its pipeline network in the state of New South Wales.
AGL said initially only the largest contract gas users, able to obtain supplies of gas independently of AGL, would have the right to seek access.
"That customer group is expected to have access rights before the end of the year, then progressively smaller customers will have the same rights over the next three to four years," AGL said.
Third party access to AGL's New South Wales gas distribution network is part a national programme to deregulate the gas and electricity markets in Australia.

AGL said users of over 500,000 gigajoules (GJ) of gas a year would gain access this year and users of over 100,000 GJ/year by July 1997. Users of over 10,000 GJ/year would have access by July 1998 and all other customers would likely gain access from late 1999/2000.
AGL said a typical domestic gas user used about 25 GJ/year.
The access undertaking only dealt with one component of the delivered cost of gas, AGL said, the cost of distribution.
"That component will fall by an average of 30 percent in real terms over the next three years," AGL said.
AGL said assuming a typical industrial contract customer could source gas and haulage at the same price as AGL, that customer would see a saving of about 6 percent a year on their delivered price.

"We are confident that the new competitive environment will see a larger natural gas market with lower overall energy prices as field price margins come under pressure," AGL's managing director, Len BLeasel, said in a statement.
Bleasel said AGL would continue to provide a competitively priced full service operation delivering natural gas from field to end user as a complete package.

"In our opinion the New South Wales (NSW) government should not have moved unilaterally to introduce open access the NSW system without first gaining full acceptance of the National Access Code and agreement with all other states for its planned introduction," Bleasel said.
Bleasel said he urged the federal government and all other states to accelerate the the finalisation of the National Access Code and the introduction of suitable legislation around the country.

The NSW government body supervising the undertaking, the Independent Pricing and Regulatory Tribunal (IPART), said it would seek public comment on the draft determination of the undertaking before issuing a final determination by the end of the year.
